title: DOJ Deploys Rare Legal Loophole in Third Attempt to Charge Ex-FBI Chief James Comey
snippet: Federal prosecutors filed a criminal information under seal to pause the statute of limitations on a 2016 leak probe, sparking outrage from legal experts and defense counsel.
content:
WASHINGTON — In an unprecedented legal maneuver, the Justice Department has launched a third attempt to criminally prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, utilizing a rarely seen procedural tactic to bypass a grand jury and pause an expiring statute of limitations.

According to recently unsealed court filings, federal prosecutors are seeking to charge Comey with two counts of violating the Espionage Act. The charges stem from an October 2016 article published by The New York Times concerning federal email surveillance. The DOJ alleges Comey improperly directed staff to disclose national defense information to reporters to correct media reporting.

An Unconventional Legal Tactic

Rather than securing a grand jury indictment or issuing a standard criminal complaint, prosecutors filed a "criminal information" under seal shortly before the 10-year statute of limitations expired. A Justice Department spokesperson defended the filing, claiming it is an established federal court practice used to toll time limits during an ongoing criminal investigation.

However, defense attorneys and former federal prosecutors expressed surprise at the move, calling it extraordinary in a contested felony matter. Criminal informations are typically utilized when a defendant has reached a plea agreement and agreed to waive a grand jury indictment.

"I have never heard of proceeding by information to toll the statute of limitations," said Michael Bromwich, a former DOJ inspector general. "This seems to be a way to do an end-run around the statute of limitations and keep a case alive that deserved to die nine years ago. This is just absolutely bizarro world stuff."

Prior Investigations Yielded No Charges

Comey's lead attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, strongly rejected the allegations, stating that the former FBI chief "steadfastly maintains his innocence." Fitzgerald highlighted that federal authorities previously investigated the leak on two separate occasions—first under Special Counsel John Durham and later under a DOJ probe code-named Tropic Vortex—with both investigations closing without charges.

In a video statement addressing the move, Comey characterized the filing as "an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to." He added, "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

Escalating Feud and Legal Precedent

The sealed court documents were made public by U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden following a request from Comey’s legal team. Judge McFadden stated that criminal proceedings involving a former FBI chief carry high public interest and noted that Comey had already offered to self-surrender if necessary.

This case represents the third effort by the Justice Department to bring criminal charges against Comey. A previous indictment accusing him of lying to Congress was dismissed by a judge over improper prosecutor appointments, while a second indictment in North Carolina—alleging Comey threatened President Trump via a social media post showing seashells arranged as "86 47"—remains pending.

When questioned by reporters on Monday evening, President Donald Trump referred to Comey as a "dirty cop" but maintained he had no prior knowledge of the Justice Department's latest filing.
